Arkansas imposes income tax on every resident, individual, trust, or
estate. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-201. Despite this broad language,
income tax would not be due when a grantor of a trust is not the
owner of property subject to a trust. Therefore, the Department
promulgated Rule 4.26-51-102 of its Comprehensive Individual
Income Tax Regulations to clarify when a grantor of a trust should
be deemed the owner of property subject to a trust. Rule 4.26-51-
102 states "A trust whereby the grantor retains control over the
income or corpus (trust property) or both, to such an extent that the
granter will be treated as the owner of the property and its income
for income tax purposes. The general result is that the income from
a grantor trust is taxable to the grantor, as "owner" of the trust, and
not to the fiduciary. In determining whether a trust is a grantor
trust, the grantor's degree of control over the trust must be
analyzed." Rule 4.26-51- 102 further instructs to look to " IRC Sec.
671 et seq." for guidance on this question.
26 U.S.C. § 675(4) states, "The granter shall be treated as the owner
of any portion of a trust in respect of which . . . [a] power of
administration is exercisable in a nonfiduciary capacity by any
person without the approval or consent of any person in a fiduciary
capacity. For purposes of this paragraph, the term "power of
administration" means any one or more of the following powers:
(A) a power to vote or direct the voting of stock or other securities
of a corporation in which the holdings of the grantor and the trust
are significant from the viewpoint of voting control; (B) a power
to control the investment of the trust funds either by
directing investments or reinvestments, or by vetoing
proposed investments or reinvestments, to the extent that
the trust funds consist of stocks or securities of
corporations in which the holdings of the grantor and the
trust are significant from the viewpoint of voting control;
or (C) a power to reacquire the trust corpus by
substituting other property of an equivalent value.
(emphasis added).

The taxpayers have never disputed that federal law required them
to be treated as the owners of the trust property. In fact, the
taxpayer reported the income on their 2016 federal return. Exhibit
3. Because the taxpayers clearly believe that for federal income tax
purposes they fall within the language of 26 U.S.C. § 675(4), the
only question that remains is whether they fall within the language
of 26 U.S.C. § 675(4) for Arkansas Income Tax purposes.
For these reasons, the taxpayers cannot claim that the Department
has not met its burden of proof. The Arkansas General Assembly
has clearly stated that trust income is subject to tax. Ark. Code Ann.
§ 26-51-201. The Department has issued a rule to clarify when the
grantor of a trust should be treated as the owner of the property
subject to trust. The trust agreement retained in its grantors the
power to control its investments and to substitute trust corpus
property. Because of this retention of power, the taxpayers are to
be treated as the owners of the trust. Therefore, the trust gains they
reported on their 2016 federal income tax return are subject to tax
in Arkansas.
For the same reasons, the taxpayer's next two arguments (i.e. that
Arkansas has not enacted any law regarding taxation of grantor
trusts and the Department's regulation regarding grantor trusts is
invalid) also fail. The Arkansas General Assembly imposed upon the
Department a broad mandate to tax "all trusts." By necessity, this
broad language requires first determining whether the grantor of a
trust should be treated as its owner. The Department has sought to
address that question in a reasonable way by adopting 26 U.S.C. §
675(4) in its Comprehensive Individual Income Tax Rules. These
rules, which were promulgated twenty-one years ago, have never
been overruled and there exists no basis on which to overrule them
here.
Finally, the taxpayers argue that imposition of a tax without
legislative authority constitutes an illegal exaction under the
Arkansas Constitution. See Art. 16 Sec. 13 Ark. Const. This
argument fails because the taxpayers do not challenge the legality of
the Arkansas income tax; they merely challenge the authority of the
Department to apply the tax to a transaction.
The Arkansas Supreme Court and Court of Appeals have considered
and denied the illegal exaction argument of the taxpayers multiple
times. Since at least 1931, the Court has held that unless the
underlying tax is itself is illegal, there can be no illegal exaction suit.
See Beard v. Wilcockson, 184 Ark. 349 (1931) ("The right of the
taxpayer to maintain this suit is predicated upon section 5786,
4

Crawford & Moses' Dig., which provides that: ‘The chancellor may
grant injunctions and restraining orders in all cases of illegal or
unauthorized taxes and assessments by county, city or other local
tribunals, boards or officers.’ . . . But the taxes here sought to be
enjoined are neither illegal nor unauthorized. They may be
excessive, but this fact alone does not authorize interference with
the collection thereof by a court of equity.") . . . The Court again in
Tucker v. Holt, 343 Ark. 216 (2000) stated, "A flaw in the
assessment or collection procedure, no matter how serious from the
taxpayer's point of view, will not make the exaction illegal; this
section was not intended to be a vehicle for such a grievance."
The Arkansas Supreme Court has been clear for nearly a century
that unless the taxpayers are arguing that Arkansas's income tax
itself is illegal, the taxpayers cannot sustain an illegal exaction suit.

ARGUMENTS
I. THE DFA HAS THE BURDEN TO PROVE THE
EXISTENCE OF A LAW TAXING THE GRANTORS
OF AN IRREVOCABLE NONRESIDENT TRUST, AND
HAS THE BURDEN TO PROVE THAT SUCH LAW
APPLIES TO THESE TAXPAYERS
While the DFA has not definitively set forth in writing the
statutory basis for its assessment, counsel for Taxpayers believes
that the DFA is attempting to tax the Taxpayers for the
undistributed income of the Trust under one or more of the
following Arkansas statutes: Ark. Code Ann.§§ 26-51-201, 26-51-
404 and 26-51-406, and Regulation 4.26-51-102. As proved below,
none of these provisions, and indeed no Arkansas law at all, permits
the DFA to tax the grantors of this nonresident trust on the trust's
14

undistributed income.
In 2015, the Arkansas General Assembly revisited the burden
of proof that applies to the interpretation of the Arkansas tax laws.
See, gen. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313. When the meaning of a state
tax law is in controversy, the burden of establishing the proper
construction of the statute is upon the party claiming application of
the tax. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313(d). Here, that burden is placed
upon the state, which is acting by and through the DFA. Where the
state seeks to impose a tax under the terms of a state tax law, then
the statute imposing the tax must be strictly construed in limitation
of the imposition of the tax. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313(a).
Where, as here, the Taxpayers are not claiming an exemption
from a tax, but rather claiming that a tax could not be levied upon
the Taxpayers, the DFA has the burden of proving the propriety of
the tax, and all doubts and ambiguities are resolved in favor of the
Taxpayers. See id. See also Leathers v. A & B Dirt Movers, Inc.,
311 Ark. 320, 325, 844 S.W.2d 314, 216 (1992); Dunhill
Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. State, 295 Ark. 483, 749 S.W.2d 666
(1988); Central and Southern Co. v. Weiss, 339 Ark. 76, 3 S.W.3d
294 (1999). Separate from the burden that applies to the
application and interpretation of Arkansas' tax laws, when it comes
to matters of fact and evidence, the burden of proof is that of a
preponderance of the evidence. Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-52-313(c).
Thus, the DFA has the burden of proof to show by a
preponderance of the evidence that under its proper construction, a
law exists which taxes these Taxpayers on the 2016 income of the
Trust. The law must be strictly construed to limit any
imposition of tax, and all doubts and ambiguities about that law
must be resolved in favor of the Taxpayers. If, after consideration
of same, a well-founded doubt still exists as to the meaning of a
statute imposing a tax, the rule of strict construction requires that
the doubt be resolved against the tax and in favor of the Taxpayers.
Ark. Code Ann.§ 26-52-313(f)(2).
II. ARKANSAS HAS ENACTED NO LAW TAXING THE
GRANTOR OF A NONRESIDENT TRUST WITH
THAT TRUST’S UNDISTRIBUTED INCOME
The concept of granter trusts is not new. Unlike the
Arkansas General Assembly, the federal government has enacted
laws which under certain circumstances tax grantors with the
income of nonresident trusts on the granters federal tax returns.
See, e.g., Sections 671-679 of Title 26 of the United States Code
("Federal Tax Code"). The precursor to those modern Federal
15

provisions was established in the Revenue Act of 1924, five years
prior to the modern enactment of Arkansas' tax law.
Since the enactment of the Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929,
the Arkansas Legislature has adopted or incorporated numerous
provisions of federal tax into Arkansas law. See, e.g., Exhibit E.
While the Arkansas legislature has had nearly 100 years to consider,
adopt or incorporate the Federal Tax Code's Sections 671-679 into
Arkansas law, and has indeed adopted hundreds of other provisions
of Federal tax law along the way, the Arkansas legislature has never
adopted or incorporated Sections 671-679 of the Federal Tax Code
into Arkansas law. Indeed, the phrase "grantor trust" appears
nowhere in the Arkansas Code. Regardless of name, the Arkansas
Code contains no law taxing the grantors of a nonresident trust with
the undistributed income of the nonresident trust. Because no such
law exists here in Arkansas, the DFA cannot meet its burden of
proof to show that an Arkansas tax law exists, and that it applies to
these Taxpayers.

I. The Director Has the Authority to Promulgate the
Grantor Trust Rules in Rule 4.26-51-102 of the
Comprehensive Individual Income Tax Regulations.
When the Arkansas General Assembly chose the language of the
Arkansas Income Tax Act of 1929, it chose extraordinarily broad
language. It chose to impose its income tax on " every resident,
individual, trust, or estate." Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-201(a)
(emphasis added). Then, it defined gross income to include
"[g]ains or profits and income derived from any source whatever."
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-404(a)(1)(E) (emphasis added). Somewhat
more specifically, it defined gross income to include "[g]ains,
profits, and income derived from dealings in property, whether real
or personal, growing out of the ownership of, use of, or interest in
the property." § 404(a)(1)(C). But even this more specific language
left open numerous obvious, yet unanswered questions.
In particular, when the Arkansas General Assembly set forth the
definition of "gross income" in Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-404, it did
not state what interests in a property are sufficient to require an
individual to report gains on the property as gross income. Clearly,
not any interest in a property is sufficient, but the General
Assembly has never drawn the line - a line that unquestionably
must be drawn somewhere.
Instead, the Arkansas General Assembly passed Act 401 of 1979,
which gave the Director of the Department of Finance
correspondingly broad authority to promulgate necessary rules for
the administration of the Individual Income Tax. See Ark. Code
Ann. § 26-51-301 (a)(1). Out of this authority and based on the
need to draw this line, the Director of the Department of Finance
and Administration ("Director") promulgated Rule 4.26-51-102 of
the Comprehensive Individual Income Tax Rules (the "Rule"),
which provides a reasonable answer to the specific question of what
interests in trust property are sufficient to subject gains on the trust
property to the definition of gross income.
For the purpose of setting forth a basis upon which to determine
what interests in a property are sufficient to require an individual to
report gains on the property as gross income, the Rule centers its
analysis around one patently reasonable consideration: control. As
it pertains to the assessment in question, the income from a grantor
trust - defined as "[a] trust whereby the grantor retains control over
the income or corpus (trust property) or both, to such an extent that
the grantor will be treated as the owner of the property and its
income for income tax purposes" - is taxable to the grantor, as
"owner" of the trust, and not to the fiduciary. Id. In determining
36

whether a trust is a grantor trust, the Rule states that the grantor's
degree of control over the trust must be analyzed. Id. To aid in this
analysis, the Rule utilizes the circumstances described in IRC § 671
et. seq. to identify when the grantor has retained such control.
Those circumstances are discussed in Part II of this Post-Hearing
Brief.
The grantor trust rules in Rule 4.26-51-102 are both reasonable and
do not run contrary to a statute. See McLane Co., Inc. v. Weiss, 332
Ark. 284, 965 S.W.2d 109 (1998) ("an agency has no right to
promulgate a rule or regulation contrary to a statute"). As stated,
the Arkansas General Assembly has not defined what constitutes a
sufficient interest nor has it defined what constitutes ownership of
property for income tax purposes. That determining the sufficiency
of the interest in a property is an essential question in determining
the applicability of the tax was not seriously challenged in the
hearing.
Further, control over the trust property is a reasonable basis for
evaluating whether an interest in a property is sufficient. While the
Taxpayers are correct that "when the state seeks to impose a tax
under the terms of a state tax law, then the statute imposing the tax
shall be strictly construed in limitation of the imposition of the tax,"
Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-313, the Director's authority to promulgate
the Rule that is necessary to clarify Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-404
comes from Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-301, which does not itself
impose a tax. For that reason, the Department's interpretation of §
301 should be highly persuasive, and it should be upheld unless it is
"clearly wrong." See Macsteel, Parnell Consultants v. Ar. Ok. Gas
Corp., 363 Ark. 22, 210 S.W.3d 878 (2005). A court will not
attempt to substitute its judgment for that of the administrative
agency. Arkansas Health Services Commission v. Regional Care
Facilities, Inc., 351 Ark. 331, 338, 93 S.W.3d 672 (2002).
To prohibit the Department - for the reasons the Taxpayers state -
from promulgating such common-sense rules such as Rule 4.26-51-
102 would have terrible consequences. For instance, the
Department could not treat the grantor of a revocable trust as the
owner of the trust's property, which CIITR 7.26-51-102 properly
directs as a matter of common sense, despite not originating in
statute. . . ..
Finally, the Taxpayers argued in their hearing that the Rule
invalidly adopted § 675 of the Internal Revenue Code because the
Director did not specify the year of the section's existence the Rule
was referring to. In so doing, the Taxpayers presumably argue that
rulemaking power has unconstitutionally been delegated to the
37

United States Congress.
This argument is misplaced for two reasons. First, in the twenty-
one years since the Rule at the heart of this assessment was
promulgated, Congress has not actually amended § 675. The
concern that one would not know what version of § 675 to apply is a
hypothetical problem. Second, the Taxpayer's argument leaves
intact the essential and operative parts of the Rule. The fact that a
portion of a regulation is void does not invalidate the whole
regulation where such portion is distinctly separable from the
remainder which in itself contains the essentials of a complete
regulation. McLane Co., Inc. v. Weiss, 332 Ark. 284, 965 S.W.2d
109 (1998). The essential parts of the Rule are (1) that a trust is
taxable to the grantor when the grantor retains control over the
income or corpus (trust property) or both to such an extent that the
grantor will be treated as the owner of the property and its income
for income tax purposes and (2) that in determining whether a trust
is a grantor trust, the grantor's degree of control over the trust must
be analyzed. These two statements themselves do not delegate any
authority. Even if the Rule made no explicit reference to the federal
statutes at IRC § 671 et. seq., their analytical framework on the
question of control over trust property would still be relevant.
The Rule being challenged in this assessment answers questions left
unanswered by the Arkansas General Assembly, is within the
Director's broad authority to promulgate necessary rules, is not
contrary to statute, is reasonable, and does not unconstitutionally
delegate legislative authority.
For these reasons, the Director of the Department of Finance and
Administration has the authority to promulgate Rule 4.26-51-102 of
the Comprehensive Individual Income Tax Regulations.

5. Did the DFA have the authority under Arkansas law adopted
by the General Assembly to tax the grantors of irrevocable non-

The incontrovertible answers to these questions are:
1. No. The General Assembly's statement in Section 1 of Act 1027
provides that "Arkansas has not previously addressed the issue of
the taxation of trusts and their beneficiaries that are grantor trusts
for federal income tax purposes".
2. No. Nowhere in the Income Tax Act of 1929 had the General
Assembly adopted any Arkansas grantor trust rules prior to the
adoption of Act 1027 in 2019. The Act is only effective for tax years
beginning January 1, 2020. Until the adoption of Act 1027,
Arkansas was one of only three states in the country that failed to
address the taxation of irrevocable grantor trusts.[Footnote 1 stated
that, “See Taxpayer’s Protest which shows that only Pennsylvania,
Tennessee and Arkansas failed to have adopted grantor trust laws
applicable to irrevocable trusts.”]
3. None. Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-102 states that it was adopted by
the General Assembly to define terms used in this "chapter", unless
the context otherwise requires. While there are twenty-six
definitions identified in Ark. Code Arm. § 26-51-102, the term
"grantor trust" is not one of them. There is no provision in Ark.
Code Ann. § 26-51-102 that enacts any statute taxing grantor trusts.
For the Department to promulgate a regulation, it must be to clarify
and interpret existing law under the Income Tax Act of 1929, as
amended. Until the adoption of Act 1027, there was no Arkansas
law taxing non-resident irrevocable grantor trusts for the
Department to interpret and clarify.[Footnote 2 was omitted] The
fatal problem for the DFA is that the issuance of Rule 4.26-51-102
to interpret and clarify the provisions of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-51-
102, which does not even mention the taxation of grantor trusts, is a
violation of the separation of powers. It usurps the legislative
function because there was simply no underlying law enacted by the
General Assembly addressing the taxation of grantor trusts that
Rule 4.26-51-102 could have been promulgated to interpret and
clarify. The Arkansas Supreme Court "will not read into a statute a
provision not put there by the General Assembly." Weiss v.
McFadden, 356 Ark. 113, 132 (2004); Oates v. Rogers, 144 S.W.2d
457, 458 (Ark. 1940) ("the functions belonging to one department
may not be usurped by the other, nor may the right to exercise such
authority be delegated.").
4. None. The DFA issued a deficiency against these Taxpayers
without even reviewing the Trust or its surrounding facts.
Had the Department reviewed the Trust and its facts before
issuing its assessment, it would have discovered that the express

terms of the Trust do not subject these Arkansas taxpayers
to Arkansas taxation on the non-resident Trust's income.
The DFA conceded in the administrative hearing that none of the

Taxpayers. The only manner in which the DFA could possibly tax
the Taxpayers on the income received by the Trust would be
through the application of the provisions of 26 U.S.C. §§ 671 et seq.
which is referenced only with the bare word "See" at the end of Rule
4.26-51-102. However, until Act 1027 was adopted those federal
law provisions were never incorporated into Arkansas law, and only
for tax years beginning January 1, 2020. The tax year at issue is
2016. The DFA cannot apply 26 U.S.C. §§ 671-679 to the Taxpayer's
2016 year, since that federal law not adopted by the General
Assembly until 2019.
5. No. The DFA asserts that it had the authority to apply 26 U.S.C.
§§ 671-679 to tax Arkansas taxpayers on the income received by
non-resident irrevocable trusts during the 2016 tax year. Why then
in 2019 did the DFA ask the General Assembly to adopt 26 U.S.C. §§
671-679 in Arkansas? The answer is in the last paragraph of the
Taxpayers' Protest: This “is a matter which addresses itself, not to
the judiciary, but to the legislative branch of
government."[Footnote 3 cited the following cases, “Comm’r of
Revenues v. Arkansas State Hwy. Comm’n, 232 Ark. 255, 258, 337
S.W.2d 665 (1960); Scurlock v. City of Springdale, 224 Ark. 408,
413, 273 S.W.2d 551 (1954).”] Representative Les Warren of Hot

and on the floor of the House, that Arkansas has been improperly

enacted any grantor trust laws. This Act enables the State to tax
non-resident granter trusts, albeit only prospectively. It was not
until this audit that the DFA discovered that the General Assembly
had never adopted any granter trust rules. The DFA's introduction
and the General Assembly's adoption of Act 1027 in 2019 is proof
positive of that deficiency and that such power to adopt federal law
lies only in the hands of the General Assembly.
Finally, Taxpayers respectfully note that ARK. CODE ANN. § 26-18-
313(1) places the burden on the DFA to prove by a preponderance of
the evidence that the taxing statute [rule] applies, (2) that the
statute [rule] imposing the tax should be strictly construed in
limitation of imposition of the tax and (3) any well-founded doubt
should be resolved against the tax. The General Assembly did not
adopt 26 U.S.C. §§ 671-679 until 2019, and only did so
prospectively. The DFA has not and cannot meet its burden to

show that the General Assembly adopted 26 U.S.C. §§ 671-679 for

CONCLUSION
Taxpayers respectfully request that the Court find that:
(A) The General Assembly's adoption of 26 U.S.C. §§ 671-679
for tax years beginning January 1, 2020 does not permit the DFA to
apply this statute to a tax year ending December 31, 2016;
(B) The DFA failed to meet its burden of proof to establish that
the language in the Rule referencing "See IRC 671, et seq.," would
result in the irrevocable nonresident Trust's gain being
taxed to these Taxpayers for the tax year ending 2016, because 26
U.S.C. §§ 671-679 was not adopted by the General Assembly for any
tax years beginning before January 1, 2020; and
(c) The Department's assessment is void ab initio. [P. 1 – 5].
Despite the numerous arguments raised by the Taxpayers regarding the
invalidity or unconstitutionality of Rule 4.26-51-102, rules promulgated under
the provisions of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-301(a)(1) (Supp. 2019) are controlling
authority for the Office of Hearings and Appeals. The Office of Hearing and
Appeals is simply not vested with the power to invalidate, overrule, or ignore
rules promulgated under the provisions of Ark. Code Ann. § 26-18-301(a)(1)
(Supp. 2019).
With respect to the applicability of Rule 4.26-51-102, the following
testimony and arguments are compelling: (1) the Taxpayers’ Witness stated that
the purpose of the reference “See IRC Sec. 671 et seq.”, in Rule 4.26-51-102, is to
bootstrap those sections up into the regulation; (2) the Tax Auditor stated that he
ultimately used IRC Sec. 675(4)(B) and (C) to determine if the Taxpayers retained

a power of administration and should be treated as the owners of the trust; (3)
the Department’s Representative contended that, “[i]n determining whether a
trust is a grantor trust, the Rule states that the grantor's degree of control over
the trust must be analyzed. Id. To aid in this analysis, the Rule utilizes the
circumstances described in IRC § 671 et. seq. to identify when the grantor has
retained such control”;17 and (4) the Taxpayers’ Representative stated that, “[t]he
only manner in which the DFA could possibly tax the Taxpayers on the income
received by the Trust would be through the application of the provisions
of 26 U.S.C. §§ 671 et seq. which is referenced only with the bare word "See" at
the end of Rule 4.26-51-102.”18 The citation to IRC § 671 et seq. and IRC Reg.
1.671-3 provides clear guidance that Rule 4.26-51-102 was intended to be read in
conjunction with the existing federal grantor trust laws and rules.
By applying IRC § 675 through Rule 4.26-51-102, the Department correctly
determined that the Trust was a grantor trust. The Taxpayers’ “power of
administration” (as defined by IRC § 675) satisfied the control requirement of
Rule 4.26-51-102. The income of the Trust was properly imputed to the
Taxpayers pursuant to Rule 4.26-51-102. The arguments raised by the
Taxpayers, regarding the invalidity or unconstitutionality of Rule 4.26-51-102,
are beyond the scope of this administrative review.
